nameStory: The West Atlantic Mantis Shrimp gets its name from its resemblance to a praying mantis, with powerful front claws that fold up like the insect's prayer-like arms. Despite the name, it's not actually a shrimp at all, but belongs to its own unique group called stomatopods. The 'West Atlantic' part simply tells us which ocean it calls home.
description: The West Atlantic Mantis Shrimp is a fascinating marine creature that looks like a cross between a lobster and a praying mantis. These robust crustaceans typically grow 6-10 inches long and have a flattened, segmented body with powerful raptorial claws used for striking prey. Their eyes are mounted on stalks and can move independently, giving them incredible vision. They're skilled burrowers that create elaborate tunnels in sandy or muddy ocean floors.

idTips.label: Raptorial Claws
idTips.description: Two large, folded front claws that look like a praying mantis's arms, with sharp spines along the inner edge that feel razor-sharp to touch

idTips.label: Flattened Body
idTips.description: Body is noticeably wider and flatter than a lobster's, with a smooth, almost rubbery texture when handled

idTips.label: Stalked Eyes
idTips.description: Large, bulging eyes on moveable stalks that can look in different directions independently, appearing almost alien-like

idTips.label: Tail Fan
idTips.description: Broad, fan-shaped tail with sharp spines along the edges that can deliver a painful cut if grabbed carelessly

idTips.label: Segmented Abdomen
idTips.description: Six distinct segments on the abdomen, each with swimming appendages that feel feathery when touched

habitat: Look for West Atlantic Mantis Shrimp in shallow coastal waters with soft, sandy or muddy bottoms where they can dig their burrows. They prefer areas 10-130 feet deep along the continental shelf from Cape Cod south. You're most likely to encounter them in fish markets, brought up by trawlers, or occasionally washed up on beaches after storms.

seasonality.spring: Most active as waters warm, with individuals emerging more frequently from burrows to hunt at night.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're most likely to be caught by fishermen and found in local seafood markets.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to reduce surface activity as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Least active, spending most time deep in burrows, rarely encountered except by deep-water fishing.

funFact: Mantis shrimp have the most complex eyes in the animal kingdom, capable of seeing 16 different types of color receptors (humans only have 3), and can actually see circular polarized light - a ability so advanced that scientists study their eyes to improve satellite and DVD technology!
confusionNotes: Often confused with lobsters or large shrimp, but the folded raptorial claws are the dead giveaway - no true shrimp or lobster has those distinctive 'praying mantis' arms. Remember: if it looks like it's praying, it's probably preying (on fish)!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'shrimp,' mantis shrimp are more closely related to lobsters and crabs, and belong to their own unique order called Stomatopoda. They're sometimes called 'thumb splitters' by fishermen due to their powerful, lightning-fast strike that can easily cut an unwary handler.
compareHints: The West Atlantic Mantis Shrimp is the only mantis shrimp species commonly found in New England waters. Compared to other mantis shrimp species found in warmer waters, it's relatively drab in coloration (lacking the bright greens and reds of tropical species) and is adapted for cooler water temperatures. Its closest relatives in our region would be lobsters and crabs, but the raptorial claws immediately distinguish it from any of these.
